575.title: Jatayu
575.hook: a prince gives a dying bird the rites of a son
575.howItsDone: Hindu funeral rites (antyeshti) are usually performed by a son or close relative; some teachers tell Rama's rites for Jatayu as a sign that loyalty can make someone family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jatayu. The old vulture broke Ravana's bow and chariot, and lost his wings for a promise. Did you keep the small promise you'd half forgotten? Day five hundred seventy-five.

Rama comes back from killing the deer, meets Lakshmana on the path, and knows before he gets there. The hut is empty. Valmiki lets Rama come apart. He runs from tree to tree asking where she went. He asks the river. He asks the deer, and the deer turn and look south. His grief turns to rage, and he says he'll tear the worlds apart, until Lakshmana talks him down. Then, on the ground ahead, they see something huge, and bleeding.
screen: `THE EMPTY HUT.` → `THE DEER LOOK SOUTH.` → `SOMETHING ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: At first Rama thinks it's a demon that has eaten Sita, and he draws his bow. Then the bird speaks. It's Jatayu, and he's dying. With what breath he has left, he tells them: Ravana took her. I fought him. He cut me down and flew south. He tries to say more. Valmiki has him begin: Ravana, son of Vishravas, brother of Kubera, the lord of wealth. And then the words stop, and he dies. Jatayu spends his last breath the way Sita spent her voice, on the message. Then Rama speaks. Holding the body, he tells Lakshmana that this bird lived long in the forest and has died for them, and that he deserves the same honor as their own father. Remember, Rama wasn't there when Dasharatha's body was burned. He heard the news in the forest, from Bharata. Now, here, Rama builds a pyre himself and performs the last rites for a vulture, as a son would. He offers the water and speaks the verses, and Valmiki says Jatayu goes to the highest worlds. A vulture king's death gets a prince's rites. And the first thing Rama does after learning who took Sita isn't revenge. It's a funeral. Before he hunts the one who took her, he honors the one who tried to save her.
screen: `A DEMON? NO: JATAYU, DYING.` · `HIS LAST BREATH: THE MESSAGE.` · `A SON'S RITES FOR A BIRD.` · `A FUNERAL BEFORE REVENGE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind someone who helped you and is gone, or far away, or simply never thanked. Let their face come up. Breathe in, and remember one thing they did. Breathe out, and let the thanks be there, unspoken, even if they'll never hear it. If nobody comes to mind, think of a stranger who once did you a small kindness. The bell holds the time.
Jatayu. His last breath goes to the message, and Rama burns him on a pyre with a son's rites.
Your line: Jatayu. Today, thank someone who tried to help you, even if it didn't work out. Day five hundred seventy-five.

576.title: Kabandha
576.hook: a headless giant with a mouth in its belly and arms that sweep the forest
576.howItsDone: Kabandha's encounter is a favorite in storytelling and temple carvings, where he is shown as a headless figure with a face on his belly and long arms.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jatayu's last breath, and a prince who gave a bird a son's funeral. Did you thank someone who tried to help? Day five hundred seventy-six.

The brothers head on through deep forest, and the forest gets stranger. Then the path is blocked by something Valmiki describes like a nightmare. It's as big as a hill. It has no head and no neck. Its mouth is in its belly, huge, with teeth. A single eye sits in its chest. And it has two arms so long they sweep the forest around it for anything to eat. Before the brothers can turn, those arms close around them both.
screen: `DEEPER INTO THE FOREST.` → `NO HEAD, A MOUTH IN ITS BELLY.` → `THE ARMS CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Its name is Kabandha, and as an ordinary Sanskrit word, kabandha means a headless trunk, a body without a head. The creature squeezes them and says, plainly, you'll do for my dinner. Lakshmana is frightened, and Valmiki lets him be. He tells Rama: leave me as its food, save yourself, and go find Sita. Rama doesn't take that offer. Instead the brothers look at each other and see the answer at the same moment. The creature's whole strength is in those arms. So Rama cuts off the right arm and Lakshmana the left, with their swords, together. The giant crashes to the ground. That's the first idea: when you're caught, look for where the strength actually is. The second comes right after. Lying there armless, the creature asks: who are you? When he hears it's Rama, his tone changes completely. He's glad. He says he's been waiting for this. He wasn't always like this, he tells them. There's a story behind the shape, and he'll tell it, but first he'll need one more thing from them. Third, notice the pattern these days are making. An old bird gives everything. A monster turns out to be waiting for help. The forest book keeps showing us that out here, nobody is quite what they look like at first: not the holy man at the door, and not the horror on the path.
screen: `KABANDHA: A HEADLESS TRUNK.` · `LAKSHMANA: LEAVE ME, SAVE YOURSELF.` · `CUT THE ARMS, WHERE THE STRENGTH IS.` · `THE MONSTER IS GLAD.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your arms rest on your thighs, heavy. Notice where you hold tension today: shoulders, jaw, hands. Breathe in, and find the one place gripping hardest. Breathe out, and let that place go a little. Don't fight the whole body. Just loosen the one grip, the way the brothers went straight for the arms. Come back to it each time it tightens. The bell holds the time.
Kabandha. A headless trunk, all arms and belly, until the brothers cut off the arms.
Your line: Kabandha. Today, when something has you in its grip, look for the one place where its strength really is. Day five hundred seventy-six.

577.title: Kabandha
577.hook: the monster's shape was a prank that became a curse
577.howItsDone: Ramayana tellers treat Kabandha's release as a turning point: from here, Rama's search runs through allies in the forest, and the curse ends through Rama's sword and a proper funeral.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabandha, the headless trunk whose arms swept the forest, cut free by two swords. Did you find where the grip really was? Day five hundred seventy-seven.
screen: `CUT THE ARMS, WHERE THE STRENGTH IS.`

segments.voice: Lying armless on the forest floor, the creature that tried to eat them sounds almost grateful. Kabandha tells the brothers his story, and it isn't a monster's story at all. Once, he says, he was radiant and beautiful, as bright as the moon. And he had a habit. He liked to put on a terrifying shape and jump out at the sages in the forest, to frighten them. One day he frightened the wrong sage.
screen: `ALMOST GRATEFUL.` → `ONCE, BEAUTIFUL.` → `A PRANK ON THE SAGES.`

segments.voice: The sage was named Sthulashira, and he was not amused. Since you love that shape so much, he said, keep it. Kabandha begged, and the sage softened the curse: it would end the day Rama cut off his arms and burned his body in the forest. There was more trouble after that. Kabandha, proud of his strength, attacked Indra, the king of the gods, and Indra's thunderbolt drove his head and thighs down into his body. That's why he has no head. So the first idea: the shape he wore as a joke became the shape he was stuck in. What we pretend to be, the story suggests, can harden into what we are. Second: he asks for a funeral. Burn me, he says, and then I'll be able to tell you how to find Sita. So once again Rama and Lakshmana build a pyre, this time for a creature who tried to eat them. From the fire, Kabandha rises in a bright form, in shining clothes, in a chariot drawn through the air. Third: his advice, and it's practical. You need a friend, he tells Rama, someone in trouble like your own. Go to the lake called Pampa and the mountain called Rishyamuka. A monkey named Sugriva lives there, driven out by his brother Vali. Make friends with him. He'll help you search. And on the way, Kabandha adds, there's an old woman of the forest named Shabari. She's been waiting for you.
screen: `A SAGE'S CURSE: KEEP THAT SHAPE.` · `INDRA'S THUNDERBOLT.` · `BURN ME, AND I'LL TELL YOU.` · `FIND SUGRIVA; VISIT SHABARI.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of a role you sometimes put on that isn't quite you: the tough one, the one who's always fine, the one who never needs anything. Breathe in, and notice how it feels to wear it. Breathe out, and set it down for these two minutes, like a costume over a chair. Just sit as yourself, with nothing to prove. The bell holds the time.
Kabandha. Cursed to keep the frightening shape he wore as a prank, freed by fire, and full of good advice.
Your line: Kabandha. Today, notice one mask you wear out of habit, and take it off once. Day five hundred seventy-seven.

578.title: Shabari
578.hook: an old woman of the forest who waited years for one visit
578.howItsDone: Shabari is honored as a model of devotion (bhakti) that needs no rank or learning; the berry story is told in later Ramayanas, songs and sermons, and some temples and festivals honor her.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabandha rose from the fire and pointed the way: Sugriva, and an old woman named Shabari. Did you set one mask down? Day five hundred seventy-eight.

On the western shore of Lake Pampa there's a hermitage that has outlived its teachers. The sages who lived there, disciples of the great rishi Matanga, have all left this world. One person stayed behind: an old woman, an ascetic, living alone among the trees. Before they went, her teachers told her that Rama would come here one day, and that she should wait for him. She has been waiting a long time.
screen: `A HERMITAGE BY LAKE PAMPA.` → `THE TEACHERS ARE GONE.` → `ONE WOMAN WAITS.`

segments.voice: Her name is Shabari. Valmiki calls her a shramani, a woman ascetic, and some readers hear in her name the Shabaras, a forest people. When the brothers arrive, she rises, bows at their feet, and welcomes them the way the old texts describe: water for their feet, water to rinse the mouth, a seat. Rama asks her the questions you'd ask any respected elder. Has your practice gone well? Have you mastered anger? Are your vows kept? Is your mind at peace? Then she answers, and here's the first idea. She says, in effect: today my practice has borne fruit, because I've seen you. She has gathered forest fruits for him, and she offers them. Second idea: look at who is honoring whom. Rama is a prince of Ayodhya. Shabari is an old woman living alone in the forest, with no rank at all. The text makes no speech about it. It just shows a prince sitting in her hermitage, asking about her inner life, and receiving what she gives him. Third, the story told in many homes: that Shabari tasted each berry first, so only the sweet ones went to Rama, and he ate them gladly. It isn't in Valmiki. It grew in later tellings, in regional Ramayanas, songs and sermons. In Valmiki she simply offers the fruits she gathered. Both are worth knowing: what the old text says, and what later devotion added to it.
screen: `SHABARI, A WOMAN ASCETIC.` · `MY PRACTICE HAS BORNE FRUIT.` · `A PRINCE IN A FOREST HERMITAGE.` · `THE TASTED BERRIES: A LATER TELLING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and picture someone who has waited a long time for something good. Maybe it's you. Breathe in, and feel the waiting: not impatient, just steady. Breathe out, and let it be enough to keep the place ready, the way Shabari kept the hermitage and gathered the fruit. You don't need to know when. Just sit, ready. The bell holds the time.
Shabari. The forest ascetic who waited at Matanga's hermitage, and said her practice bore fruit the day Rama came.
Your line: Shabari. Today, give someone the best of what you have, even if it's small and simple. Day five hundred seventy-eight.

579.title: Shabari
579.hook: flowers that never withered, and the forest book closes
579.howItsDone: Shabari's hermitage is remembered at sites near Pampa, by Hampi in Karnataka, and elsewhere; pilgrims visit places linked to her, and the Aranya Kanda is often read or recited as its own unit.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shabari, who waited for years, and offered Rama the fruits she'd gathered. Did you give someone your best small thing? Day five hundred seventy-nine.

Shabari's work isn't finished when Rama arrives. She has one more thing to do: show him the place. Here Valmiki's Shabari is less a hostess than a guide. She walks the brothers through the forest her teachers left behind, as if she's handing over the keys before she goes. It's the tour an old caretaker gives before handing over a house: this is where the light comes in, this door sticks, this is the room where we used to sing. Shabari isn't showing off. She's making sure the place is remembered properly.
screen: `ONE MORE THING TO DO.` → `A GUIDE, NOT A HOSTESS.`

segments.voice: She shows them Matanga's forest. Here, she says, is the altar where my teachers made their offerings. And look: the flowers they offered haven't withered, after all these years. Here is a place they called the seven seas. When the old sages grew too frail to travel to the sacred waters, they called the seven seas here by the power of their thought. In this telling, a holy place keeps the memory of those who prayed in it. The garlands stay fresh; the waters stay near. Then Shabari asks Rama's leave for something. I want to leave this body, she says, and go to the sages I served. Rama gives it. She enters a fire, and rises from it radiant, in shining clothes and ornaments, and goes to the world where her teachers are. She had been waiting for one meeting. When it came, her work was done, the way a long piece of work is done, and she could go. And here, beside Lake Pampa, the Aranya Kanda, the forest book, ends. Look at how it ran. Sages in their hermitages. Panchavati. Shurpanakha and the battle with Khara. Maricha's warning and the golden deer. The abduction, Jatayu, Kabandha, and Shabari. It began among sages and it ends with a sage's student. In between, nearly everything was lost. Tomorrow a new book opens, the Kishkindha Kanda, by a lake in spring, and someone is about to come down a mountain to talk.
screen: `THE ALTAR, THE UNWITHERED FLOWERS.` · `THE SEVEN SEAS, CALLED BY THOUGHT.` · `SHE RISES FROM THE FIRE.` · `THE FOREST BOOK ENDS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of a place that holds a memory for you: a kitchen, a temple, a bench, a grandparent's porch. Picture it in detail. Breathe in, and let the people who were there come to mind. Breathe out, and let the place stay as it is, still keeping what happened there. Just sit in it for two minutes, like a visitor being shown around. The bell holds the time.
Shabari. She shows Rama her teachers' forest, then leaves this world through fire, and the forest book ends.
Your line: Shabari. Today, show someone a place that matters to you, or tell them its story. Day five hundred seventy-nine.

screen: `DAY 579 COUNTS.` → `THE FOREST BOOK, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: HANUMAN'S FIRST WORDS.`

580.title: Hanuman's first words
580.hook: a frightened king, two strangers with bows, and a careful messenger
580.howItsDone: Hanuman is worshiped across the Hindu world; in Valmiki he first appears here, as Sugriva's counselor and messenger, and devotees who recite the Kishkindha Kanda meet him in this scene.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shabari, and the end of the forest book. Did you show someone a place that matters? Today the Kishkindha Kanda begins. Day five hundred eighty.

Spring at Lake Pampa. Lotuses, bees, birds calling, trees heavy with flowers. And Rama, standing at the shore, finds it unbearable. The Kishkindha Kanda opens on a man surrounded by beauty, and every bit of it reminds him of the person who isn't there. He talks to his brother about it at length, the flowers, the breeze, the birds, and none of it helps. Lakshmana listens for a long time. Then he says, gently, enough. Grief like this will wear you down. Let's go.
screen: `SPRING AT LAKE PAMPA.` → `BEAUTY THAT HURTS.` → `LAKSHMANA: LET'S GO.`

segments.voice: Meanwhile, up on a mountain called Rishyamuka, someone is watching. Sugriva, the exiled monkey prince, sits there with four counselors. He sees two men, armed with bows, walking straight toward his hiding place, and he panics. He's sure his brother Vali has sent them to kill him. That's the first idea. The kanda doesn't begin with a hero meeting a hero. It begins with fear. Sugriva is a hunted man, and two strangers with bows look like the end. So he turns to his wisest counselor, and that's Hanuman. Hanuman calms him first. You're jumping at shadows, he tells him, more or less, and a king who acts on fear before he knows is a weak king. Then Sugriva gives him the job. Go down and find out who they are. Watch their faces, their speech, their manner. Tell me if they mean harm. Second idea: how Hanuman goes. Not as a monkey. He takes the form of a wandering mendicant, a bhikshu. Sound familiar? Only days ago in the story, Ravana came to Sita disguised as a holy man, to deceive and to steal. Now Hanuman takes nearly the same disguise, to find out the truth and to protect. The same costume, opposite hearts. Third: look at who Hanuman is in this first scene. Not the giant who leaps the sea, not yet. A careful messenger walking down a mountain, deciding what to say. Tomorrow we hear the words.
screen: `SUGRIVA SEES TWO ARMED MEN.` · `HANUMAN CALMS THE PANIC.` · `A MENDICANT'S DISGUISE.` · `SAME COSTUME, OPPOSITE HEARTS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and recall the last time a stranger made you nervous. Notice what your body did: the tight chest, the fast guesses. Breathe in, and let that memory come up. Breathe out, and soften it. You don't have to decide whether the fear was right. Just practice the pause Hanuman gave Sugriva: a breath between seeing and deciding. The bell holds the time.
Hanuman's first words. Not spoken yet: today he's sent down Rishyamuka, in a mendicant's form, to find out who the strangers are.
Your line: Hanuman's first words. Today, before you decide what someone means, find out. Ask one real question. Day five hundred eighty.

581.title: Hanuman's first words
581.hook: a stranger's sentence so well made that Rama names every virtue in it
581.howItsDone: Devotees honor Hanuman for learning and eloquence as well as strength, and this passage, where Rama praises his grammar and delivery, is one source of that picture.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman's first words, still unspoken. A mendicant walking down a mountain to meet two strangers. Did you ask before deciding? Today the week closes. Day five hundred eighty-one.

Have you ever met someone and known within a minute, from how they spoke, that you could trust them? Not from what they said, exactly. From how. That's today. Hanuman reaches the brothers and speaks, and when he's finished, Rama turns to Lakshmana and says something remarkable about a stranger's sentence. Remember where Rama is. He has lost his kingdom, his father and now his wife. He has no reason to trust anyone on this mountain. And a few sentences from a stranger change that.
screen: `NOT WHAT, BUT HOW.` → `RAMA TURNS TO LAKSHMANA.`

segments.voice: Hanuman greets them with respect. You look like sages, he says, or like kings: why are you in this forest? Then he tells them who he is: a minister of Sugriva, a monkey king driven out by his brother, who wants their friendship. He's careful and warm, and he tells the truth about who sent him. Then Rama turns to Lakshmana, and his praise is precise. Nobody could speak like this, he says, who hadn't learned the Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda and the Sama Veda. He has clearly studied grammar well; in all he said, not one word was wrong. Nothing in his face, his eyes or his brow was out of place. He didn't drag it out or rush it. His voice came from the chest and throat, in a middle pitch, clear and pleasing. A king with a messenger like this, Rama says, can get anything done. First idea: when Rama meets Hanuman, what he praises is his speech. Not his strength. Second: good speech here is a kind of goodness. Not slick, not showy: right in length, right in tone, honest about who sent him. Third: Rama is grieving and exhausted, and he still notices a stranger's care with words, and says so. Now the week, from the top. Jatayu's last breath and his funeral. Kabandha, and the curse that came from a prank. Shabari, waiting, and the flowers that never withered. Lake Pampa in spring. And today, a sentence that starts a friendship.
